strengths: Combining BORE-style class-probability acquisition with label propagation and label spreading is a plausible, useful contribution. The method accommodates both supplied candidate pools and continuous domains where unlabeled points are generated, and its relationship to TPE, BORE, LFBO, and graph-based semi-supervised learning is clearly acknowledged.

The evaluation covers four synthetic functions, four tabular optimization benchmarks, three NATS-Bench datasets, and an image-based search task, with ten repetitions. The reported curves show substantial improvements on several synthetic problems and faster convergence on NATS-Bench against multiple BORE/LFBO classifiers and GP acquisition functions.

The supplementary ablations examine kernel bandwidth, unlabeled sample count, sampling distribution, and pool subsampling. The comparison without unlabeled data is particularly useful evidence that adding these points can improve optimization in the tested settings.

The overall algorithm is understandable, with pseudocode, propagation equations, and supplementary descriptions of baseline architectures and search spaces. These provide a useful foundation for further investigation.
weaknesses: The theoretical argument in Section 4.3 does not establish the claimed advantage for the proposed algorithm. Equations (11)–(13) concern minimax bounds and the existence of a semi-supervised learner under particular assumptions; they do not show that the chosen label-propagation/spreading procedures attain those bounds. The required separation between the bounds is not established for the studied problems, and classification-risk improvement is not connected to acquisition maximization or optimization regret. Consequently, the superiority statement following Equation (8) is unsupported. The analysis should either establish an applicable result or be explicitly limited to motivation.

The central explanation involving the cluster assumption and overconfidence remains unverified. Sampling truncated Gaussians around evaluated points does not ensure that high-density connected regions share an objective-threshold label; a threshold boundary can pass directly through such a region. Generated points can supply a useful smoothing bias, but their construction does not establish the assumed relationship between geometry and labels. Moreover, the qualitative Branin illustrations do not demonstrate that enlarging the high-probability region improves exploration or prevents local trapping. The two-function ablation without unlabeled points is helpful but does not isolate this mechanism from bandwidth effects and randomized tie-breaking.

Important implementation details remain unspecified even in the supplement. These include the main benchmark settings or selection procedures for β and α, propagation tolerances and iteration limits, default pool subsample sizes, and input normalization and categorical encodings. Section S.4 shows substantial bandwidth sensitivity, making these omissions consequential. The stated use of L-BFGS-B with 1,000 initializations also leaves unclear how finite-pool constraints are enforced and how acquisition optimization is handled for tree-based baselines. These gaps prevent confident reproduction and assessment of comparison fairness.

The experiments support promise more strongly than broad superiority or practical scalability. All continuous benchmarks are two-dimensional, and random search is absent despite the randomized selection heuristic and large evaluation budgets. Dense graph construction has quadratic storage requirements, yet no runtime or memory comparisons quantify the effects of subsampling and acquisition optimization. The plotted uncertainty bands are also undefined, and several tabular results finish close to strong baselines. Numerical summaries with clearly specified uncertainty and computational costs would make the contribution substantially easier to assess.

The MNIST experiment has a significant interpretation limitation. Section S.3.4 trains the embedding network on 440,000 images labeled with the exact three-digit target, achieving 96.9% test classification accuracy. Although the search pool uses held-out images and the embeddings are shared across methods, this supplies extensive supervision directly relevant to the optimization objective. The experiment therefore demonstrates search within a strongly supervised representation. A baseline ranking candidates using the pretrained classifier's predictions, together with an accounting of the auxiliary supervision, is needed to establish the additional value of Bayesian optimization on this task.

There are smaller mathematical presentation errors that should be corrected. The entrywise definition of P in Section 4.1 is column-normalized, whereas the stated matrix expression D⁻¹W is row-normalized; Equation (6) then uses P transposed, making the intended update ambiguous. Equation (9), presented as a normalized density, also omits the Gaussian normalization constant. These are secondary to the unsupported theoretical and experimental conclusions above.
